..
Issued at 158 PM CDT Thu Sep 17 2026

A diffuse front/differential heating zone in the vicinity of
I-90/88 continues to slowly work its way southward early this 
afternoon. To the north of the boundary, persistent low stratus 
has held temperatures in the upper 60s and lower 70s, while to 
the south temperatures have warmed into the upper 80s. This 
boundary will continue to ooze southward through the rest of the
afternoon and evening. As it does so, low-level saturation 
depths are forecast to increase a bit along and north of I-80 as
a modest trailing mid-level shortwave passes by overhead. This 
may be sufficient to crank out some showers or drizzle at times.
Ahead of the front, some showers or storms may develop late 
this afternoon and into the evening as lingering convective 
inhibition erodes following peak heating. Low-level convergence 
along the boundary doesn't look particularly robust however, and
this may end up being a limiting factor in terms of any 
convective coverage. As modest low-level isentropic upglide 
continues atop the sagging frontal zone, additional showers and 
a few storms may continue to fester through the evening south of
I-80. 

Conditions look to remain largely dry within the post-frontal  
airmass tomorrow. However, some guidance does suggest the surface 
baroclinic zone may slosh back northward just far enough to 
push the elevated instability layer back across our far south 
and west locales during the afternoon. Have included a slight 
chance of storms to account for this potential, but most 
guidance suggests this boundary should remain south of the CWA. 
Some additional spotty showers can't be ruled out across 
northern Illinois ahead of the next developing storm system. 

Attention then shifts to what looks like another period of 
occasionally stormy weather in the region over the weekend, with
an increasing threat for heavy rainfall and at least a 
localized flash flood threat. Several mid-level impulses will 
slingshot around the eastern periphery of a broad and persistent
upper-level trough across the western CONUS Friday night into 
Saturday morning. This in turn will induce cyclogenesis across 
the Central Plains. As this occurs, intensifying southwesterly 
flow will overtop the surface baroclinic zone, resulting in a 
significant expansion of rain and embedded thunderstorms across 
the Upper Midwest. Increasing upper divergence within the right 
entrance region of a fast anticyclonic jet streak, coupled with 
broad and fairly intense WAA/upglide within a richly-moist 
airmass characterized by essentially record PWATs north of 2 
inches will facilitate the potential for embedded heavy 
training convective elements with torrential rainfall. While 
some uncertainty in the exact placement of the salient 
baroclinic zone and low track remains, extended CAM and coarse-
resolution ensemble guidance continues to pain the greatest 
heavy rain probs roughly near/north of I-88 late Friday night 
through Saturday morning. Conceptually, the set up is a 
concerning one from a flash flood potential, although the most 
persistent jet divergence/deepest moisture may set up just north
and west of our CWA--still to be determined though. 

With AM convection decidedly elevated, the severe threat appears  
low. CAMs hint at the potential for some elevated Gravity Wave 
Associated Convection (GWAC), but meager MUCAPE/DCAPE should 
curtail the threat for severe gusts in the area. 

It's a bit unclear where the surface boundary will reside
Saturday afternoon. With widespread morning convection, the 
boundary may have a difficult time making it meaningfully back 
into our forecast area (suspect the latest ECMWF remains a bit 
too far north). In this scenario, any additional afternoon 
activity should generally be of the light-moderate shower 
variety. However, a second wave is forecast to shift overhead 
Saturday night into Sunday, and may result in another round of 
locally heavy rainfall nearly across the same areas. 

Have issued a Hydrologic Outlook for areas roughly along and
north of I-80 given the potential for two rounds of heavy 
rainfall. May need consider Flood Watch(es) for parts of the 
area if confidence in training convection continues to increase.
Some shower activity may linger into Monday, but high pressure 
is forecast to build into the region towards the middle and end 
of next week. 

Carlaw
